questions.q: Why does the lesson say presenting to a non-specialist audience is NOT just 'the technical talk, simplified'?
options: The goal is replacing precise-but-opaque technical language with precise-but-accessible plain language, not removing detail or accuracy
Because non-specialist audiences should receive less accurate information
Because non-specialist talks should never include any actual numbers
Because simplification and translation mean the same thing in this context
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly distinguishes removing detail (the wrong goal) from replacing jargon with accessible-but-still-accurate language (the right goal).

questions.q: In the worked plain-language translation, how was the 0.155 error reduction (from a 0.240 baseline) described?
options: The correction technique cut the number of wrong measurements by about two-thirds
The correction technique had no measurable effect at all
The correction technique doubled the error rate
The correction technique was described using only the raw decimal numbers with no translation
questions.explain: 0.155 divided by the 0.240 baseline is about 0.646, which the lesson rounds to 'about two-thirds' -- an accurate, accessible translation of the same number, verified by direct calculation.

questions.q: Why does the lesson specifically warn against translating 'the hardware's physical imperfections caused some measurements to come out wrong' as simply 'the computer made a mistake'?
options: That phrasing undersells the real statistical/probabilistic, partly predictable and partly correctable nature of the phenomenon
Because 'mistake' is a forbidden word in any quantum computing talk
Because computers never make any kind of error
Because this translation is too long for a non-specialist audience
questions.explain: The lesson explains this shorter phrasing overstates certainty by making it sound like a simple binary error, when the real phenomenon is probabilistic and partly correctable -- accuracy should be preserved even while simplifying language.

questions.q: What honest caveat does the worked plain-language example give for the non-specialist audience, and how does it compare to the technical-audience limitations slide?
options: It states only two sizes and one device were tested, so the pattern can't yet be claimed to hold more broadly -- the same scope limit as the technical talk, in accessible language
It omits any mention of limitations, since non-specialist audiences don't need them
It claims the result definitely holds for all future, larger quantum computers
It states the result is completely unreliable and should be disregarded
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states the same scope limits should be given to both audiences, just in accessible rather than technical language -- not omitted, and not overstated or completely dismissed.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say overselling is a SPECIFIC risk with non-specialist audiences, more than with technical audiences?
options: A non-specialist audience often can't independently check a quantum computing claim the way a technical peer could, shifting the burden of honest framing onto the presenter
Because non-specialist audiences are more likely to be hostile to the claims
Because technical audiences are incapable of detecting overselling
Because non-specialist talks are never recorded or reviewed by anyone
questions.explain: The lesson explains that because non-specialists can't independently verify technical claims, the presenter bears more responsibility for honest framing -- directly connecting to the popular 'breakthrough' overselling problem flagged back in Lesson 1.
